overview.title: Jewish Drohiczyn Through Its Memorial Book
overview.summary: Drohiczyn’s Jewish community was a place of religious learning, schools, family life, trade, culture, and political debate. The memorial book follows this life through periods of imperial rule, war, migration, German occupation, murder, hiding, and survival. It also shows how survivors and landsleit gathered names, photographs, testimonies, and documents after the destruction. Exploring these paths will help readers understand both the community that was lost and the work of remembrance that keeps its people present.

paths.title: What made Jewish Drohiczyn a community?
paths.description: This path introduces the institutions, livelihoods, families, and everyday relationships that shaped Jewish life in Drohiczyn. By the end, readers will see the community as a living society rather than only as a place later destroyed.
paths.question: How did Jewish people study, worship, work, and build family life in Drohiczyn?

steps.title: Religious institutions and communal care
steps.summary: Before the First World War, Drohiczyn had four study houses and a Hasidic prayer house. The Chevra Kadisha also organized burial rites and cemetery care, showing how religious life involved both worship and communal responsibility.

steps.title: Schools and Jewish education
steps.summary: Jewish residents secured permission for a school in 1883, and it opened in 1885 with 52 boys and many girls. Later institutions included the Moriah and Yavne schools, linking Jewish education with both traditional and modern cultural goals.

paths.title: How did Drohiczyn’s Jews respond to a changing world?
paths.description: This path follows cultural, political, and migratory changes from the late nineteenth century into the First World War. It shows how religious scholarship, libraries, Zionism, socialism, and emigration all became part of community life.
paths.question: How did education, politics, and migration reshape Jewish Drohiczyn?

steps.title: A culture of learning and books
steps.summary: Drohiczyn’s religious culture included a yeshiva founded in 1905 and traditions of commentary on works such as Mishnat Hasidim and Lehem Mishneh. The Workers’ Library, photographed in 1910, shows that communal learning also extended into organized secular culture.

steps.summary: Some Drohiczyn Jews left for America, while others moved toward the Land of Israel; Litman Eisenstein, for example, went to America in 1890 and later returned. These movements connected the town to New York, Palestine, and other Jewish communities without ending local family and communal ties.

paths.title: What happened to the community under occupation?
paths.description: This path moves from wartime control and coercion to ghettoization, murder, and the destruction of families. It emphasizes the memorial book as a collection of survivor accounts and documentary traces, not as an all-seeing independent narrative.
paths.question: How did German occupation transform Jewish life into persecution and mass murder?

steps.title: Occupation brought coercion and fear
steps.summary: The memorial book describes German authorities imposing demands through a Jewish Council and demanding gold and a large monetary contribution. Other accounts describe German soldiers forcing residents into labor and pursuing them, showing how occupation penetrated everyday life.

steps.title: The ghetto and communal endurance
steps.summary: Under German rule, the Burial Society continued to function in the ghetto and held annual meals. Its activity suggests that even under persecution, communal obligations and religious care remained important to those imprisoned there.

paths.title: How did people survive, resist, and begin again?
paths.description: This path follows individual and family strategies of survival, armed resistance, migration, and postwar organization. It shows that the story did not end with destruction, while also recognizing the immense losses carried by survivors.
paths.question: What forms did survival and rebuilding take after persecution?

steps.summary: One account says that Petruk’s family was hanged for hiding Shimon Kravets. Another describes children hiding with the narrator in swamps, illustrating both the danger faced by rescuers and the desperate conditions in which some people sought refuge.

paths.title: How did survivors preserve Drohiczyn?
paths.description: This path examines the memorial book as an act of testimony, collection, and communal responsibility. Readers will learn how names, photographs, documents, publications, and personal accounts were assembled to resist disappearance.
paths.question: How can a destroyed community be remembered through a memorial book?

steps.title: The yizkor book as a memorial project
steps.summary: The volume presents itself as a Drohitchin yizkor book and was assembled from collected raw material and photographs. Its purpose was to offer friends and readers a memorial to the community, combining remembrance with historical reconstruction.
